learningObjectives: Explain what the TBox framework is and what problem an automation framework solves.
Describe how Engines 3.0 sit on top of TBox and steer their respective technologies.
Distinguish GUI engines from non-GUI engines and give examples of each.
Explain how an XModule carries engine information and how the familiar authoring model coexists with technology-specific supported actions.
Reference a specific table row by value ($) or by index (#), and narrow a TestStep to one row with Constraint.
Describe how TC Shell and the Tosca REST API let you inspect and drive a Tosca project without opening Tosca Commander.

elements.description: Each technology exposes different interfaces. A shared framework supplies common automation building blocks while engines implement technology-specific operations.

The Tosca TBox framework is the .NET-based foundation that all Engines 3.0 are built on, for both GUI and non-GUI tests. It provides one common interface across every supported technology, so the differences between technologies are absorbed by the Engine rather than pushed up into your TestCases. TBox and its Engines 3.0 are part of the standard Tricentis Tosca installation — nothing extra to install for the core engines.

elements.text: The original Tosca 16.0 theory names five architecture benefits: performance in authoring/execution, a common technology interface, XScan/Recorder-assisted authoring, shared dynamic-expression behavior and a broader ActionMode range. These are source claims about the framework, not a guarantee of equal supported actions or measured speed for every target.

bulletPoints: The framework's job is to make 'steer a web button' and 'steer an Excel cell' look the same to the person building the TestCase.
TBox is standard — it ships with Tosca, it is not a separate product.

elements.description: An Engine is the technology-specific layer that knows how to find and manipulate controls in one kind of application. It translates the generic instruction coming from the TestCase — 'set this value', 'verify this value', 'click this' — into whatever that particular technology actually requires.

elements.title: Engines you will meet across Tosca (AE1 covers the non-web ones)
items: XBrowser Engine 3.0 — web applications across Chrome, Edge, Firefox (the AS1/AS2 territory).
Excel UI Engine 3.0 — the Microsoft Excel user interface: application window, dialogs, and loaded worksheets.
Excel Engine 3.0 — workbook/file manipulation, distinct from Excel UI steering of the application.
PDF Engine — PDF documents, including comparison reporting between files.
Mail Engine 3.0 — mail automation; supported protocols, account authentication and Module-specific restrictions need separate checks.
UIA Engine 3.0 — Windows controls via the Microsoft UI Automation framework.
WinX Engine 3.0 — Windows UI API applications; distinguish it from legacy Win32 steering.
Mobile engines — inspect version-specific native and mobile web support and prerequisites.
API Engine 3.0 — web services and API endpoints (the API Testing course's territory).
Plus technology-specific engines outside AE1's scope: SAP, Java, Salesforce.

elements.text: The original interactive overview has seventeen Engine information cards across three pages. Its broad technology descriptions are for the course-era overview; they do not certify current driver, platform, protocol, licensing or authentication compatibility. Microsoft UI Automation is the underlying framework; do not confuse its authorship with the Tosca UIA integration.

bulletPoints: AE1's lesson list is essentially a tour of the non-web engines: Excel, PDF, Mail, UIA/WinX, Mobile.

elements.description: Steer something a human could see and click: a browser page, an Excel worksheet, a Windows dialog, a mobile screen. Identification is about locating a visible control.

Steer backend systems with no visual component — the XML and JSON engines, API calls, protocol-level interactions. There is no screen to look at; the Engine works directly against the data or the service.

elements.text: TBox deliberately supports both categories through the same framework. That is what allows a single TestCase to, for example, submit a web form, then verify the resulting record via an API call, then check that the confirmation PDF was generated correctly.

bulletPoints: GUI = there is a control to find on a screen. Non-GUI = there is data or a service to address directly.
Both share TBox authoring concepts and can be combined when the selected Modules, prerequisites and execution environment are compatible.

elements.description: Engines 3.0 use XModules to steer test objects. An XModule is the Tosca object that represents a piece of the application under test, and it carries the information the Engine needs to find that object again at execution time. XModules can be structured hierarchically and referenced across many TestCases — the same reuse model you already know from web automation.
A Module carries engine/interface information used by its TestSteps. Scanned and Standard Modules can represent different technologies; inspect the actual Module configuration.
Modules, TestSteps and TestStepValues remain familiar building blocks. Available ActionModes depend on InterfaceType and control support; they are not universally identical for every engine.

bulletPoints: Module → Engine → technology. You choose the Module; the Engine follows automatically.
Check supported ActionModes for the Module interface and control.

elements.description: The original Tosca 16.0 prerequisite exercise creates a single-user workspace named AE1 Exercises using AE1_Base_Subset.tsu as its workspace template. This prepares the supplied training objects; it is not a recommendation to use single-user storage for every production team.

items: Obtain the original AE1_Base_Subset.tsu from the course attachments.
In Tosca Commander, create a new single-user workspace named AE1 Exercises. Enable Use Workspace template and select the supplied base subset, then confirm creation.
Once creation finishes, inspect AE1 Exercises > Modules > Standard modules > TBox XEngines for the supplied engine Modules, including Excel, PDF and Mail.

elements.text: These names and navigation are scoped to the original course installation. Confirm the workspace and Module tree actually exist; reading the instructions or source subset is not a runtime test. The original framework checklist contains one self-assessment objective about exploring the applicable Engines, not a graded test of successful workspace creation.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Bonus: steering a specific table row

elements.term: Header-relative positions, absolute positions and value constraints
elements.description: For rows without cell constraints, $ identifies positions relative to the configured header and # identifies absolute positions. With cell constraints, #2 can select the second matching row. Neither notation means searching by a business value on its own; configure constraints and the intended occurrence explicitly.

A steering parameter that tells Tosca which row of the scanned table holds the column headers. Once set, later TestStepValues can address a column by its header text instead of a raw column number — 'the Total column' rather than 'column 4' — which keeps the TestCase readable and keeps it working if columns are reordered but not renamed.

Constraint filters rows by one or more cell values. Choose a unique business match or deliberately select a matching occurrence before verifying or buffering another cell; the constraint alone does not guarantee uniqueness.

elements.text: Row and cell values in a table TestStep also accept REGEX instead of a literal string, so a row can be matched by pattern — a date, an order number with a variable suffix — rather than an exact value that would otherwise have to be hardcoded and would break on the next test run.

The original 2022 Table Steering guide was compared in full, including seven exercise stages and every screenshot. Its prepared shopping cart demonstrates header offsets, duplicate-product occurrence selection and REGEX alternatives. These source expected results do not certify execution against the current shop.

elements.description: In the source cart, $1 addresses the first data row while #1 can address the header. Setting HeaderRow to 2 makes the named Product(s) header unavailable; positional column selection demonstrates the offset instead. Removing HeaderRow makes $ and # behave alike in that example. After restoring the header, a product-name constraint with #2 selects the second matching Music 2 row, not the second physical cart row.

bulletPoints: $ positions are header-relative; # positions are absolute without constraints or identify a matching occurrence with constraints.
Use business-value constraints when row order can change.
HeaderRow defines which row supplies headers; inspect uniqueness before acting.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Bonus: operating Tosca outside Tosca Commander

elements.description: TC Shell is the command-line control of Tosca Commander itself — it lets you navigate a Workspace, read or modify a TestStepValue, and run an ExecutionList entirely from the command line, without the Tosca Commander UI ever opening. It has two modes: interactive, where you type commands one at a time and get the same range of functions the GUI offers; and script, where a batch of commands is read from a script data file with no opportunity to intervene — the mode built for running an extensive test portfolio unattended, for instance from a CI pipeline.

Open TC Shell with the workspace path and authentication appropriate to its repository type. Parameters are case-sensitive. JumpToNode uses an object NodePath; task lists operations available for the current object. Inspect the applicable start/command documentation rather than assuming every repository uses -login.

Pass a plain-text .tcs command file to start script mode. Supply task inputs in that file; TC Shell processes commands, closes the workspace and exits. A wrapper is optional, not an intrinsic requirement of script mode.

The public 2026.1 TC Shell reporting workflow requires a report definition with designer configuration and PrintOutputFormat set to NONE. Navigate to the data object, run its Print Report task, and supply the output location/name/type. This is a TC Shell workflow; the original course REST example below uses a different PrintOutputFormat. Neither workflow guarantees the expected file solely from HTTP status.

items: For the original optional text-file exercise, prepare its supplied subset in a training workspace and run the initial TestCase to establish the output file. Record the Text TestStepValue and target ExecutionList NodePath from their properties.

Close Commander before opening that workspace through TC Shell. Navigate to the recorded value, inspect its available tasks, choose Modify Value, provide the requested inputs, then navigate to the ExecutionList and run it.
In script mode, provide the navigation, modification inputs, execution and Save operation in the .tcs file. Use the actual workspace and script locations; a batch wrapper is one launch option.
Check the execution result and resulting text-file contents. A completed shell command alone does not prove the expected data was written.

elements.text: The 2023 hands-on guide illustrates particular task menu numbers and a local-repository login. Choose the available task by name/current menu, confirm repository-specific authentication, and use ordinary straight quotes and actual NodePath values. Its training paths and expected results are source examples, not evidence of a fresh run in this environment.

elements.description: The 2023 course guide requires matching Tosca/Tosca Server versions, the REST service and its WorkspaceBasePath configuration. It selects an ExecutionList with existing results, records its UniqueId, sets the report definition to ASKUSER, and saves/closes Commander. Its API Scan example calls the object PrintReport task with reportName and outputFilepath and Basic authentication. Use actual configuration and repository credentials; its example port, ID and paths are not universal defaults.

elements.text: ASKUSER belongs to that original REST example; NONE above belongs to the versioned TC Shell documentation. Do not silently substitute one into the other workflow. After the response, verify the generated PDF exists and contains the intended execution details at the configured Windows output location. An HTTP 200 response alone does not certify report contents or browser download. Service activation and report execution have not been performed here.

bulletPoints: TC Shell provides interactive and script modes.
Inspect the current reporting workflow and verify the resulting file; do not infer success solely from a response code.

examPitfalls.title: Thinking each Engine needs its own way of building TestCases
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Assuming that automating Excel or PDF requires a different TestCase structure or scripting approach than web automation.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use the common object model, but inspect the engine/interface-specific operations.

examPitfalls.title: Believing TBox or Engines 3.0 are separate add-ons
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Looking for a separate installer or licence for the TBox framework.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The TBox framework and its Engines 3.0 are part of the standard Tricentis Tosca installation. (Individual technologies may still need their own prerequisites — Excel installed, a mobile agent deployed — but the engines themselves ship with Tosca.)

examPitfalls.title: Trying to assign an Engine to a TestStep manually
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Looking for an Engine dropdown on the TestStep when a control isn't behaving as expected.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Engine selection follows from the Module, which is created when you scan the application. If the wrong Engine is steering something, the fix is at the Module/scan level, not the TestStep.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming non-GUI means 'no automation possible'
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Treating backend steps as something that must be verified manually because there is no screen.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: TBox explicitly supports non-GUI engines (XML, JSON, API). Backend verification is a first-class part of an end-to-end TestCase, not an exception to it.

examPitfalls.title: Steering a table row by # when the row order can change
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Hardcoding row #7 to always mean a specific order, then having the TestCase silently check the wrong row after the data set changes.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Both $ numeric and # numeric addressing are positional. Use cell constraints with a unique business value when order varies.

examPitfalls.title: Confusing interactive and script modes
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Starting TC Shell without a script and expecting unattended command replay.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Pass the script path for script mode; without a script it starts interactively.

examPitfalls.title: Mixing reporting workflows
examPitfalls.trapDescription: An older REST example does not establish current TC Shell configuration.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The reviewed 2026.1 TC Shell workflow uses NONE on the report definition; validate the produced file.

examPitfalls.title: Assuming an API endpoint is verified
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Server reporting setup and authentication vary by version.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Consult the applicable REST API manual before using an endpoint. The original hands-on report guide was inspected, but its source-era service configuration and expected result are not a verified current endpoint or runtime result.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the role of the TBox framework in Tosca?

options.text: It is a separate licensed product for performance testing.
It is the .NET-based foundation all Engines 3.0 are built on, giving one common interface across every supported technology for both GUI and non-GUI tests.
It is the scripting language used to write Tosca TestCases.
It only applies to web application testing.

practiceQuiz.hint: Think about what makes automating Excel feel the same as automating a web page.
practiceQuiz.rationale: TBox is the shared .NET foundation for all Engines 3.0, covering GUI and non-GUI tests alike. It absorbs the differences between technologies so the TestCase-building workflow stays constant, and it ships as part of the standard Tosca installation.

optionExplanations.A: TBox is the shared automation foundation, not a performance product.
optionExplanations.B: It supplies a common framework for GUI and non-GUI Engines 3.0.
optionExplanations.C: The framework is not a mandatory test scripting language.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A TestCase contains one TestStep steering a web page and another steering an Excel worksheet. How does Tosca know which Engine to use for each TestStep?

options.text: The tester selects the Engine from a dropdown on each TestStep.
Each TestStep inherits its Engine from the Module it was created from.
Tosca tries every Engine until one succeeds.
A single TestCase cannot mix technologies.

practiceQuiz.hint: The binding happens one level above the TestStep.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Modules are bound to an Engine when the application is scanned, and every TestStep created from a Module is steered by that Module's Engine. This is exactly what lets one TestCase mix technologies with no special handling.

optionExplanations.B: The TestStep uses its referenced Module configuration.
optionExplanations.C: Engine selection is not trial-and-error execution of every engine.
optionExplanations.D: One TestCase can contain Modules for multiple technologies.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which of the following is a non-GUI engine?

options.text: XBrowser Engine 3.0
Excel UI Engine 3.0
XML Engine 3.0
Mobile Engine 3.0

practiceQuiz.hint: Which one has no screen or visible control to locate?
practiceQuiz.rationale: The XML Engine 3.0 works directly against data with no visual component, making it a non-GUI engine. XBrowser, Excel UI, and Mobile all steer visible controls on a screen.

optionExplanations.B: Excel UI operates visible application controls.
optionExplanations.C: XML processing works directly with structured data.
optionExplanations.D: The described Mobile steering targets visible application controls.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What do Engines 3.0 use to steer test objects?

options.text: XModules
ExecutionLists
Requirements
TestSheets

practiceQuiz.hint: It is the object that represents a piece of the application under test.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Engines 3.0 use XModules to steer test objects. An XModule carries the identification information the Engine needs, can be structured hierarchically, and is reusable across TestCases.

optionExplanations.A: XModules represent the objects used by Engines 3.0.
optionExplanations.B: ExecutionLists organize runs rather than object identification.
optionExplanations.D: TestSheets model test data rather than steering objects.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A table's rows are re-sorted differently on every test run, but a TestCase must always find the row for a specific Order ID. Which row-referencing approach should it use?

options.text: # — reference the row by its fixed position.
Constrain the row using its unique Order ID value before reading the target cell
HeaderRow — it replaces the need to identify a specific row at all.
Neither; re-sorted tables cannot be steered.

practiceQuiz.hint: Business-value matching differs from either kind of numeric position.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Both $ numeric and # numeric forms identify positions. A unique Order ID constraint finds the intended record despite reordering. HeaderRow establishes headers, not the required business row.

optionExplanations.A: A fixed absolute index follows position, not Order ID.
optionExplanations.B: A unique business-value constraint survives reordered rows.
optionExplanations.C: HeaderRow establishes header addressing, not record identity.
optionExplanations.D: Reordered tables can be searched by business values.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A TestStep needs to find the table row where Product = 'Laptop', then verify the Price cell in that same row. Which mechanism makes that possible?

options.text: REGEX alone, with no other setting.
The Constraint ActionMode, to lock the TestStep onto the row matched by Product before acting on Price.
The # notation, referencing the row by index.
Re-scanning the table for every possible Product value.

practiceQuiz.hint: One column locates the row; a different column is then read.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Constraint narrows the row search by Product. Ensure the match is unique, then verify Price. An index is positional and rescanning each value does not model this reusable search.

optionExplanations.A: A pattern alone does not define the required row/cell relationship.
optionExplanations.B: Constraint narrows the row before accessing Price.
optionExplanations.C: A numeric index does not identify the Laptop business value.
optionExplanations.D: A reusable table Module can search different values.

practiceQuiz.scenario: How does TC Shell enter script mode instead of interactive mode?

options.text: Keep the Commander UI open to select script mode
Pass the command script file in the start parameters
Make every workspace read-only
Start a REST API service

practiceQuiz.hint: The start command needs the script resource.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Pass the script file as a start parameter. With no script, TC Shell starts interactively. A REST service, read-only workspace or Commander UI is not the mode selector.

optionExplanations.A: The UI is not the TC Shell mode selector.
optionExplanations.B: Supplying the script path starts command replay in script mode.
optionExplanations.C: Read-only access does not select script mode.
optionExplanations.D: REST is separate from the TC Shell mode selection.

practiceQuiz.scenario: For the documented Tosca 2026.1 TC Shell reporting workflow, what output-format setting is required before printing?

options.text: Set PrintOutputFormat to NONE on the report definition
Disable all authentication
Start a REST API service; no report definition is needed
Always set ASKUSER on ExecutionEntries regardless of workflow

practiceQuiz.hint: Read the current TC Shell reporting prerequisites, not an older REST walkthrough.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Set PrintOutputFormat to NONE on the report definition for this TC Shell workflow. Authentication choices and API service state are not the requested reporting prerequisite.

optionExplanations.A: NONE is the documented report-definition setting for this workflow.
optionExplanations.B: Removing authentication is not a reporting configuration.
optionExplanations.C: A REST service does not replace the TC Shell report definition.
optionExplanations.D: The older ASKUSER claim is not the reviewed TC Shell prerequisite.

quickRecap.value: .NET-based framework underpinning all Engines 3.0; ships with standard Tosca.
One common interface across every technology — higher performance, and no per-technology workflow to relearn.
The technology-specific layer that knows how to find and manipulate controls in one kind of application.
GUI = a visible control to locate (XBrowser, Excel UI, Mobile). Non-GUI = data or service, no screen (XML, JSON, API).
The object Engines 3.0 use to steer test objects; hierarchical and reusable.
Determined by the Module, not chosen per TestStep — which is why one TestCase can mix technologies freely.
Numeric $ addressing is header-relative; # is absolute. Use unique cell constraints to find business records; HeaderRow defines headers.
Interactive mode prompts for commands; script mode processes a supplied .tcs file. Start parameters and authentication depend on repository type.
For the reviewed 2026.1 workflow: configured report definition, PrintOutputFormat NONE, Print Report task, and explicit output location/name/type. Inspect the file.
